Gagosian Booth C10 With works by Damien Hirst From Moon Kyungwon and Jeon Joonho ’s nearby seating installation, where tired visitors can take a break, the orderly dots of Damien Hirst ’s “ Spots ” paintings and centrifugal bursts of his “ Spin ” paintings come directly into view. The booth feels like the section’s unofficial anchor. Inside, those instantly recognizable paintings give way to Nemesis (2007), a clinically ordered work from the “Pill Cabinets” series, and faux archaeological relics from the “Treasures from the Wreck of the Unbelievable” series. Hirst’s MMCA survey drew more than 500,000 visitors this spring while also stirring debate over its blockbuster scale, public spending, and critical framing—perhaps fitting for an artist who has never been far from controversy. By the end of the day, the gallery had placed “significant works” from the presentation to collections including a museum in Asia. Indeed, the “Spots” and “Spin” paintings were attracting the most visitors—and camera phones. For anyone wanting to look beyond the spectacle, Gagosian’s detailed online presentation offers short texts and videos on each series. UNAW Gallery Booth S13 With works by Gyutae Hwang Photography is hard to find at Frieze Seoul this year. For its debut at the fair, UNAW Gallery joins the new Spotlight section with Korean artist Gyutae Hwang , tracing his work from the 1960s through the 2000s. The gallery’s executive director, Soyoung Ryu, emphasized Hwang’s historical importance as an early figure who continually tested the boundaries of what photography in Korea could be. title: Nan Goldin shoots Acne Studios’ 30th anniversary campaign.
summary: Acne Studios has enlisted Nan Goldin to shoot its 30th-anniversary campaign, the Swedish fashion house announced. The American photographer made a series of portraits of artists, musicians, and actors from the brand’s orbit, each dressed in denim—the material the label built its name on—in a mix of new, archival, and reissued styles from its three decades. Goldin photographed nine friends of the house: artists Jonathan Lyndon Chase , Sandra Poulson , and Peter Schlesinger ; actors Rila Fukushima and Juliette Lewis; models Raya Martigny and Guinevere Van Seenus ; musician Ellie Rowsell; and photographer Jordan Hemingway. A 10th portrait, of an unnamed friend, will follow at a later date. All the sitters have worked with the brand before: Chase designed the runway set for its Spring/Summer 2025 show in Paris, and Poulson’s sculptures have appeared in its stores. “I have been inspired by Nan and her work for years,” said Jonny Johansson, co-founder and creative director of Acne Studios, in a statement. “So, when we realized we had 30 years to celebrate, it felt like the right moment to ask her. I wanted an icon, but I also wanted something very intimate and personal. She does that.” The sitters, he added, are “individuals we have collaborated with, spoken to, or had some kind of exchange with over the years. I wanted friends, not models.” The commission is a natural fit for Goldin, who has spent five decades photographing her chosen family of friends and lovers, most famously in “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency ” (1985). In 2017, she founded the group P.A.I.N. , whose museum protests pushed institutions worldwide to drop the Sackler name over the family’s role in the opioid crisis. Laura Poitras ’s documentary All the Beauty and the Bloodshed (2022) chronicled her life and that campaign. Goldin has shot for fashion houses before, including a 2024 Gucci campaign featuring Debbie Harry and Kelsey Lu.

title: The 5 Best Booths at Kiaf SEOUL 2026
summary: Kiaf SEOUL returned to the COEX in Gangnam with a typically stylish and enthusiastic crowd on Wednesday, September 2nd. Marking a milestone 25th anniversary, the fair brings together 175 exhibitors from 18 countries under its first externally appointed creative director, designer Kuho Jung, who oversaw a rebrand built around the theme of Coexistence. This iteration promises an exploration of humanity’s shifting relationship with technology. Special exhibitions “HUMAL” and “Invisible,” the latter woven with AR works accessible by QR codes across the fair floor, extend the theme. Coexistence, it turns out, is built into the fair’s very architecture. This is also the fifth year that Kiaf shares its venue with Frieze Seoul , which takes place on the floor above. The result is a sense of fluidity and buzz; Wednesday’s throng of VIPs flitted between the two. The youthful, engaged, and excited crowd here makes the fairs feel like a festival. At one point, it was difficult to peruse Kiaf’s aisles without ending up in someone’s selfie or video. Works by international heavyweights are plentiful at Kiaf, but visitors can also leave the fair with myriad discoveries, thanks to the strong regional depth in dealers and artists. The organizers have successfully curated a neat snapshot of the Korean and regional art scene, with a smattering of global flair. “It’s the biggest platform for art in Korea,” Sunghoon Lee, the president of the Galleries Association of Korea, which runs the fair, told Artsy. “The fair’s role is to put new artists and older artists together, and Kiaf is the biggest in size, top quality, and it also has the most number of participants in Korea. We also have international galleries participating, so it is a platform for networking.” And art lovers in Seoul will have plenty to feast on beyond the COEX, as if more than 250 gallery booths wasn’t enough. The fairs anchor Seoul Art Week, which brings an enormous serving of shows and pop-ups to town. Each night this week, different neighborhoods take turns hosting a local cluster of events and openings, turning art viewing into a round-the-clock task of trying to avoid FOMO. And if that still wasn’t enough, then consider that this year’s Seoul Art Week is part of the Korea Art Festival. Some four biennales—Jeju, Busan, Gwangju, and Gyeonggi—are all taking place across the country this month, adding firepower to a week in the Korean capital that is already among the busiest in the art world. Indeed, judging by the mood at the COEX, the audience here is more than ready to take on the challenge. Here, we select our five best booths from Kiaf SEOUL 2026. Her work appears alongside that of established Korean artists Lee Kyoungmi , Hanna Kim , Hur BoRee , and Baek Kyungho . Yet it’s Hong’s oil paintings that dominate the space. They span small, jewel-like canvases to the nearly 6-foot-tall Griant (2025). title: $1.28 million Adrian Ghenie painting leads opening sales at Frieze Seoul 2026.
summary: Frieze Seoul 2026 kicked off its VIP day on Wednesday, September 2nd, at COEX. Now in its fifth edition, the fair is known for drawing a mix of collectors, curators, institutional leaders, and stylish VIPs, largely from across the Asia Pacific region. This year was no exception, with K-pop stars The8 from the band Seventeen and Annie and Bailey from AllDay Project, singer Woodz, models Hye-jin Han and Yano Shiho, and actors Ji-won Uhm, Dasom, So-Hee Han, and Si-young Lee. Adding to the initial excitement were several six-and seven-figure transactions, led by Thaddaeus Ropac ’s sale of Adrian Ghenie ’s Figure with Funerary Stele (2026), for €1.1 million ($1.28 million). “It’s fantastic to see how Seoul Art Week has matured across the city, with the impressive institutional developments and the calibre of museum exhibitions,” said gallery founder Thaddaeus Ropac. “It’s been a strong start to the fair with swift sales, largely to collectors based in Korea, but also spanning Asia—Malaysia, China, Hong Kong—and a few to European and American collectors.” Dealers also reported active institutional buying, particularly from Asia. title: Galerie Nordenhake opens new Berlin space in Charlottenburg.
summary: Galerie Nordenhake is opening a new, larger location in Berlin’s Charlottenburg district, the gallery announced this week. The space, at Goethestraße 2–3, opens to the public on September 10th with a reception timed to coincide with Berlin Art Week. A group exhibition titled “Symptoms” will be the space’s inaugural show. The move caps a year of 50th-anniversary programming for the gallery, which celebrated five decades of exhibitions across its Berlin, Stockholm, and Mexico City locations in 2026. The new address—a 19th-century building constructed in 1881 as a post office complex and designed by the architect Wilhelm Tuckermann—previously belonged to Galerie Max Hetzler . “Symptoms” brings together 16 artists who work in collage, photography, sculpture, and paint, including Mirosław Bałka , John Coplans , Ann Edholm , and Not Vital . The exhibition title links their pieces to traces of underlying conditions: The featured artists explore the unease of these subtle cues through fragmented bodies, unstable pictorial space, and hybrid materials. At the center of the exhibition is Benjamin Orlow’s Ritual City (2026), a large-scale plaster, ceramic, and wood sculpture in which two figures merge with scaffolding, which the gallery describes as “suspended between formation and dissolution.” Other works include Edvard Munch ’s 1895 lithograph Vampyr II , a grief-laden early drawing by George Grosz , and Michael Schmidt ’s nine-part photographic group Untitled (from Waffenruhe) (1985–87). The show also features paintings by Mamma Andersson and Sophie Reinhold , and collage works by Frida Orupabo drawn from archival photographs of Black bodies.

title: Your Guide to the Art World in Fall 2026
summary: Fall 2026 is stacked for the art world. Five continents’ worth of art fairs, a run of blockbuster museum openings, two major auction weeks, and more than a dozen gallery weekends are all packed into 16 weeks. The season opens in South Korea, with Frieze Seoul and Kiaf SEOUL’s milestone 25th edition in early September and closes with Art Basel Miami Beach and its satellite fairs in early December. In between there are plenty of other highlights including the Whitney Museum of American Art ’s long-awaited Roy Lichtenstein survey, the opening of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, and Frieze’s launch into the Middle East with Frieze Abu Dhabi. Below is a month-by-month breakdown of the fairs, museum shows, and other happenings worth planning around. September 2026 Art fairs in September 2026 Frieze Seoul and Kiaf SEOUL (Sep. 2–6), COEX, Seoul: Frieze Seoul enters its fifth edition alongside its partner fair Kiaf SEOUL , which marks its 25th anniversary this year under the theme “Coexistence.” Together the two fairs bring more than 300 galleries to Seoul, with Kiaf alone hosting 175 exhibitors from 18 countries and territories. A slate of citywide “Neighborhood Nights” of gallery openings and festivities runs throughout the week. Sydney Contemporary (Sep. 2–6), Carriageworks, Sydney: Australia’s largest contemporary art fair celebrates its 10th edition this year, bringing roughly 100 galleries and more than 500 artists to Sydney. Tokyo Gendai (Sep. 10–13), Pacifico Yokohama: Now in its fourth edition, this international contemporary fair splits its program across established-gallery, emerging-artist, and works-on-paper sections. It’s quickly become a key stop on Asia’s expanding fair circuit. The Armory Show (Sep. 24–27), Javits Center, New York: The 32nd edition of New York’s flagship fair brings together around 230 galleries and introduces new Caribbean Focus, Performance, and After Hours programming this year. Independent 20th Century (Sep. 24–27), Sotheby’s at The Breuer, New York: This edition marks the fair’s first at Sotheby’s new home on Madison Avenue. It’s the biggest edition of the fair yet, with 56 exhibitors and more than 130 artists spanning modern and post-war work. Three museum shows opening in September 2026 to watch The Bayeux Tapestry, British Museum , London: Opening September 10th and running through July 2027, this is the first time the nearly 1,000-year-old, 70-meter tapestry has left France . It depicts the events leading up to the 1066 Battle of Hastings, and tickets through the end of the year had already sold out following record demand. The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, Los Angeles: The museum founded by George Lucas and Mellody Hobson opens to the public September 22nd (member previews begin September 5th) in Exposition Park. Designed by Ma Yansong of MAD Architects, it houses more than 40,000 works centered on illustration and narrative storytelling . The building is more than a decade in the making. Maurizio Cattelan , “NIGHT,” Neue Nationalgalerie, Berlin: Running September 10th through March 2027, this is Cattelan’s first major solo exhibition in Germany, staged as he receives the 2026 Preis der Nationalgalerie. Curated by Lisa Botti with director Klaus Biesenbach, it will feature signature works like Him (2001) and La Nona Ora (1999)—a sculpture of the pope stricken by a meteorite —along with new commissions. Other art world happenings to know in September 2026 Berlin Art Week (Sep. 9–13): the 15th edition activates more than 100 museums, galleries, and project spaces across the German capital. Madrid Apertura Gallery Weekend (Sep. 10–13): the Spanish capital’s 17th annual season-opening weekend will feature roughly 60 member galleries. Warsaw Gallery Weekend (Sep. 18–20): the 16th edition of Warsaw’s citywide gallery weekend featuring around 60 exhibitors and over 130 artists. Barcelona Gallery Weekend (Sep. 17–20): the 12th edition, organized by Art Barcelona, will span 25 galleries across the city’s neighborhoods. RendeVous - Brussels Art Week (Sep. 10–13): Four days of exhibitions and events at over 95 venues. curated by Vienna (opening weekend Sep. 11–13, running through Oct. 17): the 17th edition of the Austrian capital’s gallery festival in which curators are invited to mount shows at galleries across the city. This year’s theme is “LOVE.” Prague Art Week (Sep. 24–27): the fifth edition, spanning roughly 100 events across 40 institutions, most with free admission. October 2026 Art fairs in October 2026 Atlanta Art Fair (Oct. 1–4), Pullman Yards: The fair’s third edition returns to the Pullman Yards venue and brings more than 70 galleries from as far afield as South Korea, Spain, and Uganda. Art Jakarta (Oct. 2–4), JIExpo Kemayoran, Jakarta: Featuring more than 70 galleries with a spotlight on Southeast Asian modern and contemporary art, Art Jakarta is also complemented by a curated program of events this year. Untitled Art, Houston (Oct. 1–4), George R. Brown Convention Center: The second edition of Untitled Art’s foray into Texas features 95 galleries. Artissima (Oct. 29–Nov. 1), OVAL Lingotto Fiere, Turin: Now in its 33rd edition, this fair, known for spotlighting experimental and cutting-edge practices, brings roughly 180 galleries from 35 countries. London Art Week The British capital comes alive in the fall, anchored by a clutch of art fairs: Frieze London and Frieze Masters (Oct. 14–18), The Regent’s Park: The flagship pair, running side by side as they do every year, with leading contemporary art at Frieze London and historical/20th-century at Frieze Masters. The free outdoor Frieze Sculpture program runs concurrently in the park from mid-September through early November. 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair (Oct. 15–18), Somerset House: The leading fair dedicated to contemporary African and diasporic art. PAD London (Oct. 13–18), Berkeley Square: The suave design-and-20th-century-fine-art fair returns to Mayfair. London Invitational (Oct. 15–18), the Chancery Rosewood: Based on a floor of one of London’s glitziest hotels, a tight roster of galleries have been corralled by the founders of the Dallas Invitational. Fair Play (Oct. 15–18), One Marylebone: New fair where selected artists receive free exhibition stands in exchange for commissions on sales. Paris Art Week Just after London Art Week, the French capital plays host to a bevy of art world activity. The slate of key fairs is as follows: Art Basel Paris (Oct. 21–25), Grand Palais: The fifth edition is the first staged under new director Karim Crippa, with 211 exhibitors from 41 countries taking part. Expect the typical Art Basel fare of blue-chip works and heavyweight artists. Paris Internationale (Oct. 21–25), location TBD: The trendy emerging art-focused fair is running for an extended period this year. Asia Now (Oct. 20–24), Monnaie de Paris: Its 12th edition, dedicated to contemporary Asian art. AKAA (Also Known As Africa) (Oct. 23–25), Carreau du Temple: Focused on African and diasporic contemporary art and design. Post-Fair (Oct. 19–24), Rue du Temple: The Paris edition of the February Los Angeles fair of the same name, this fair presents 34 solo and duo artist presentations. London and Paris October auctions: what to know Both tentpole auction weeks land alongside their respective fairs. London’s evening sales group around Frieze week (October 14th–18th), while Paris’s take place around Art Basel Paris (October 21st–25th). The 2025 London sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips were up roughly 131% year over year, so expectations will be on livelier auctions compared to seasons past. Full October 2026 lots and estates aren’t yet public at the time of writing, but Christie’s has announced that a leading lot of their London 20th/21st Century evening sale will be Piet Mondrian ’s Composition III (1920), which carries an estimate of £20 million–£30 million ($27.3 million–$40.9 million). Last year’s comparable weeks set a strong precedent, with Christie’s October 2025 London evening sale hitting £106.9 million ($145.7 million), its best Frieze Week result in seven-plus years. In Paris, Sotheby’s and Christie’s combined sales totaled €182 million ($212.3 million), including all-time French auction records for Surrealist art. Five museum shows opening in October 2026 to watch Roy Lichtenstein, “Like New,” Whitney Museum of American Art , New York: Opening October 11th (member previews Oct. 8 to 10), this survey of the post-war icon features more than 130 works spanning the 1940s through the 1990s. It’s co-curated by Meg Onli and guest curator artist Alex Da Corte . All eight works from Lichtenstein’s 1962 debut at Leo Castelli’s gallery will be reunited for the first time. Mariko Mori , “All That Shines,” Mori Art Museum , Tokyo: Opening October 31st and running through March 2027, this retrospective gathers 80 works across three decades of Mori’s practice, tracing her fusion of art, science, and metaphysics through installation, sculpture, video, and performance. “ Krasner and Pollock : Past Continuous,” The Metropolitan Museum of Art , New York: Running October 4th through January 2027, this is the first major New York presentation devoted to either artist in more than 20 years and the first at the Met for either. It features 120-plus works drawn from more than 80 lenders across 12 thematic chapters. “ The ’90s: Art and Fashion ,” Tate Britain , London: Running October 8th through February 2027 and curated by former British Vogue editor in chief Edward Enninful, this show brings together more than 100 works—including photography, painting, film, sculpture, and fashion—from nearly 70 artists. Salman Toor , “Someone Like You,” The Courtauld, London: Running October 2nd through January 2027, this is Toor’s first solo exhibition in Europe. It will feature 19 paintings made since 2019 alongside a selection of drawings. Other art world happenings to know in October 2026 Rome Art Week (Oct. 19–25): The nonprofit, artist- and gallery-organized citywide festival now draws over 700 participating artists, who open their studios directly to visitors, alongside galleries, foundations, museums, and academies hosting exhibitions, talks, and performances. Everything is free. November 2026 Art fairs in November 2026 Art Cologne (Nov. 5–8), Koelnmesse, Cologne: Founded in 1967 and widely regarded as the world’s oldest modern art fair, this 59th edition remains a bellwether for the German and Central European market, blending blue-chip 20th- and 21st-century galleries with emerging positions. Art X Lagos (Nov. 5–8), the Federal Palace: West Africa’s first international art fair (launched in 2016) remains a leading spot for contemporary African and diaspora art, drawing galleries and collectors from across the continent and beyond. Art Collaboration Kyoto (Nov. 7–9), Kyoto International Conference Center: Now in its sixth edition, ACK’s distinctive format pairs each Japanese gallery with an overseas counterpart in shared booths, prioritizing cultural exchange. West Bund Art & Design and ART021 (Nov. 10–15), Shanghai: The two flagship fairs of Shanghai Art Week, these fairs are key barometers of the Chinese contemporary art market. Paris Photo (Nov. 12–15), Grand Palais: The 29th edition coincides with the “Bicentennial of Photography” and brings together roughly 242 exhibitors—195 galleries and 47 publishers—from 38 countries, making it the world’s leading fair dedicated to the photographic medium. Art Mumbai (Nov. 12–15), Mahalaxmi Racecourse: Now in its fourth edition, this fair has quickly become a key fixture in South Asia for modern and contemporary art, spanning historic Indian modernism through current practices. ADAA Fair, New York (Nov. 13–16), Park Avenue Armory: The Art Dealers Association of America rebranded its long-running “The Art Show” as the “ADAA Fair” for this edition after a one-year hiatus, naming 63 exhibitors, timed to New York's marquee November auction week. Frieze Abu Dhabi (Nov. 19–22), Manarat Al Saadiyat: This inaugural edition marks Frieze's first venture into the Middle East, with Deutsche Bank as global lead partner—one of the season’s biggest launches. Two museum openings in November 2026 for your radar Self-Portrait, 1952-c. Vanessa Bell Piano Nobile Sophie Calle , Hamburger Bahnhof , Berlin: Opening November 13th (through May 2027) as part of the museum’s 30th-anniversary celebrations, this is the French artist’s first Berlin solo show in more than 20 years, spanning six bodies of work across three decades. It includes a new work commissioned for the anniversary that will enter the museum’s permanent collection as a donation. “ Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant : Inside Bloomsbury,” Tate Britain, London: Opening November 12th (through April 2027) in partnership with Charleston, the Bloomsbury Group couple’s former Sussex home and studio, this is the first major exhibition to chart their intertwined artistic and personal relationship. It features more than 300 works and a full-size re-creation of Grant’s studio, relocated from Charleston for the show. New York November 2026 auctions: what to know New York’s November week remains the fall’s marquee auction moment for Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips, running the 20th- and 21st-century evening sales that anchor the global auction calendar. Specific 2026 headline lots and consignments haven’t been announced as of late August 2026, but Artnet News revealed last month that Sotheby’s has secured the $450 million Blaquier collection, with works by Vincent van Gogh , Paul Cézanne , and Edgar Degas . Auction house catalogues typically go public in September and October. For scale, the equivalent sales last year were up 77% year over year for the three houses. Expect a competitive week. Other art world happenings to know in November 2026 Art Week Tokyo (Nov. 4–8): The fifth edition of this citywide initiative activates more than 50 museums and galleries. Lisbon Art Weekend (Nov. 5–8): A citywide gallery and institution weekend reflecting Lisbon’s growing profile as a Southern European art hub. December 2026 Art fairs in December 2026: Miami Art Week Arguably the busiest week of fairs in the U.S. art world calendar , Miami Art Week takes place hot on the heels of Thanksgiving. Art Basel Miami Beach (Dec. 2–6), Miami Beach Convention Center: This year is expected to draw the usual mix of blue-chip galleries and major collectors that has made it the most influential fair in the Americas since its 2002 launch. Other fairs to note: Design Miami (Dec. 1–6), Pride Park: Now in its 22nd edition, this is a leading fair for collectible design, bringing historical and contemporary furniture, lighting, and objects from galleries worldwide. NADA Miami (Dec. 1–5), Ice Palace Studios: The New Art Dealers Alliance’s 24th edition brings together 135 galleries and has long served as the go-to slot for emerging and mid-career dealers. Untitled Art, Miami Beach (Dec. 2–6), beachfront pavilion on Ocean Drive: In its 15th edition with 160-plus galleries, it’s known for its purpose-built beachfront tent and a curatorial approach that mixes emerging and established galleries side by side. Pinta Miami (Dec. 3–6), The Hangar: Marking its 20th anniversary this year, it remains the leading fair dedicated to modern and contemporary Latin American art. SCOPE Miami Beach (Dec. 1–6), Miami Beach: With more than 80 international galleries, it’s built around discovering emerging artists and has run alongside Art Basel Miami Beach since 2002. A museum opening in December 2026 for your radar Guggenheim Abu Dhabi: Two decades after the project was first announced in 2006, the Department of Culture and Tourism—Abu Dhabi and the Guggenheim Foundation have set an opening date of December 11, 2026, for the monumental Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. Designed by the late Frank Gehry , the 800,000-plus-square-foot building—with the architect’s signature motif of cone-shaped galleries—will be the largest Guggenheim institution in the world. It will contain roughly 125,000 square feet of exhibition space across 30 galleries.

title: Princess Diana exhibition to premiere at Ronald Reagan Presidential Library.
summary: The Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Museum will open “Princess Diana: Love Life Legacy—A Life of Giving” on November 7th—the exhibition’s global premiere. The show runs through May 31, 2027, at the Simi Valley, California, institution and brings together more than 700 artifacts from Diana’s life. They range from childhood keepsakes to the fashions that made her a global icon. Centerpieces include the “Travolta” dress, which Diana wore while dancing with John Travolta at a 1985 White House state dinner and is on loan from Historic Royal Palaces, and the “Final Goodbye” dress—Diana’s last collaboration with designer Jacques Azagury, who created some of her best-known pieces. Other highlights include her iconic “Black Sheep” sweater, the “Caring” dress she wore visiting hospitalized children, her wedding slippers, the official program from her 1981 wedding to Prince Charles (now King Charles III ), and a run of Lady Dior handbags, jewelry, letters, and personal documents. “This exhibition offers an intimate look at one of the most memorable chapters in modern diplomatic history,” said Melissa Giller, chief marketing and cultural programming officer of the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute, in a statement. “The Reagan Foundation is honored to be the first location to host the exhibit, showcasing the deep bond between Princess Diana and the Reagans, as well as the timeless influence that Princess Diana shared with the world.” Future venues are yet to be announced. Diana and the Reagans forged a public friendship during the Reagan presidency, capped by her 1985 Washington D.C. visit and her widely photographed dance with Travolta. She died in a car crash in Paris in 1997, a year after divorcing Prince Charles. In recent years, prices for Diana’s wardrobe have climbed steadily at auction—a 1985 Jacques Azagury gown made $1.1 million in 2023, a Victor Edelstein gown made $910,000 in 2024. And last year Julien’s Auctions’ “Princess Diana’s Style & A Royal Collection” sale in Beverly Hills brought in more than $5 million. Several lots that day landed far past their estimates: a Catherine Walker coat dress sold for $455,000 against a $50,000 high estimate, and a Lady Dior handbag brought $325,000 against an estimate of $30,000.

title: 11 Must-See Museum Shows to See in Fall 2026
summary: As summer draws to a close, museums around the world are unveiling lineups of not-to-be-missed exhibitions. Some are righting long-standing gaps in the canon: The Denver Art Museum spotlights the resilience of Indigenous artists across Latin America, Helsinki’s Ateneum traces the overlooked role of esotericism in women artists’ work, and Tate St Ives mounts the first definitive retrospective of renowned British modernist painter Wilhelmina Barns-Graham . Others speak to the present. As the U.S. celebrates 250 years of independence, Taryn Simon unveils a sprawling Guggenheim installation tracing a father’s decades in government service; at the New Museum , Arthur Jafa ’s survey mines internet culture, social media, and popular music to reveal the many layers of contemporary Black life; and Hong Kong’s M+ museum explores how fantasy shapes our understanding of the world today. This season brings both sweeping retrospectives of household names and showcases for rising artists, which take center stage from New York to Accra. Below are 11 must-see museum shows this fall. Taryn Simon “Father Country I Do Love You” The Guggenheim , New York Sep. 18, 2026–Mar. 14, 2027 American artist Taryn Simon is known for highly researched projects that draw attention to overlooked stories from across the globe. Her photographic series “The Innocents” (2000) traced the lives of wrongfully incarcerated individuals, while her sonic and sculptural installation An Occupation of Loss (2016) highlighted professional mourners performing grief rituals. Simon’s interactive installation for the Guggenheim, titled “Father Country I Do Love You,” features an entirely new body of 42 artworks that includes photography, text, video, and sculpture. Altogether, they chart the life of an unnamed federal agent. He bears some resemblance to her own mysterious father, who traveled the globe on assignment for the U.S. government, then settled into a second life selling arcade games. Simon developed the project over roughly a decade, and it marks the first time she’s woven personal narrative into her practice. Simon’s father received an Alzheimer’s diagnosis before he could divulge his full story to his daughter, who turns to art and invention to fill in the blanks. Through the lens of her speculative protagonist, the artist offers a sprawling web of stories shaped by one man's life in service of a nation. This is the first solo presentation by a photography-focused artist to occupy the Guggenheim’s rotunda, and the largest debut of new work in the museum’s history. Arthur Jafa “I Am Tony” New Museum , New York Sep. 24, 2026–Jan. 3, 2027 For over three decades, Arthur Jafa has made cinematic art about the reality of being Black in America. The Mississippi-born artist has engaged with internet culture, social media, cinema, and music as he’s built a remarkable archive of images exploring themes of race and identity. Jafa often employs collage and montage to create “affective proximities” (a concept coined by his longtime collaborator, Ghanaian British artist John Akomfrah ) that reveal the intersections of history, violence, culture, and entertainment. “I Am Tony” at the New Museum is the largest exhibition of the artist’s work to date, featuring early and new pieces in photography, installation, painting, and sculpture alongside a selection of Jafa’s most acclaimed videos, including Love is the Message, The Message is Death (2016) and The White Album (2019), winner of the Golden Lion at the 2019 Venice Biennale. Named after the famous jazz drummer Tony Williams, the show traces the evolution of Jafa’s cinematic creations, which echo the texture, styles, and themes of Black popular music. “I Follow Rivers: Indigenous Worlds in Latin America” Denver Art Museum , Denver Nov. 8, 2026–July 27, 2027 For centuries, colonial violence has threatened the dignity and survival of Indigenous groups across modern-day Latin America. “I Follow Rivers: Indigenous Worlds in Latin America” spotlights the resilience of these communities, many of whom turn to art as a form of resistance. The largest exhibition in the United States dedicated to modern and contemporary Indigenous Latin American artists, the show will present more than 100 works by over 50 artists. They include internationally acclaimed names such as Sheroanawë Hakihiiwe , Abel Rodríguez , MAHKU (Huni Kuin Art Movement) , and Denilson Baniwa. The works on view will illustrate the cultural richness and enduring strength of Indigenous peoples throughout Latin America as they touch on themes such as land, community, history, and change. Highlights include textiles by Claudia Alarcón ; a major installation by Claudia Martínez Garay ; and delicate works on paper by Hakihiiwe. John Baldessari “The End of the Line” Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM) , Miami Through May 9, 2027 Pioneering Conceptual artist John Baldessar i favored ideas and linguistic play throughout his work. Drawing on text, found photography, film stills, advertising, and appropriated imagery, he undermined notions of authorship, originality, and the way images communicate meaning. Baldessari was also a beloved CalArts instructor who cemented his place as a defining figure of the Los Angeles art scene. Among his best-known works are series in which he covered his subjects’ faces with colored dots to strip away identity and celebrity. “If you can’t see their face, you’re going to look at how they’re dressed, maybe their stance, their surroundings,” he said during an NPR interview in 2013. “John Baldessari: The End of the Line” at the Pérez Art Museum Miami will showcase nearly 40 works of painting, photography, video, and installation by the Californian artist, spanning five decades. Drawn from the Craig Robins Collection, the pieces are organized across three sections, spotlighting the artist’s earliest works, his serial and experimental photographic methods, and his boundary-breaking dialogue with mass media and popular culture. Gala Porras-Kim “El movimiento de un registro fluvial (The Motion of an Alluvial Record)” Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (MAMM), Medellín, Colombia Sep. 9, 2026–Mar. 28, 2027 In her multidisciplinary practice, Gala Porras-Kim examines how museums categorize, preserve, and interpret their collections. Born in Bogotá, now based between Los Angeles and London, the artist critiques efforts to halt natural decay and the passage of time; this mindset clashes with how other cultures understand and discuss the meaning of objects. “El movimiento de un registro fluvial (The Motion of an Alluvial Record)” at the Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (MAMM) marks the artist's first institutional show in Colombia. Featuring drawings, installations, and institutional dialogues, the exhibition questions Western approaches to conserving, representing, and safeguarding cultural property. Standout works on view include 62 Offerings for the Rain at the Palacio Cantón (2023), a graphite and colored pencil drawing from Porras-Kim’s ongoing series depicting ritual artifacts excavated from the Sacred Cenote of Chichén Itzá, and Out of an Instance of Expiration Comes a Perennial Showing (2022), a textile that features mold spores propagated from the British Museum and reflects on themes of growth and collection storage. Wilhelmina Barns-Graham Tate St Ives, Cornwall, England Oct. 24, 2026–May 3, 2027 A key figure of British modernism, Wilhelmina Barns-Graham moved to St Ives, in Cornwall, in 1940 and became a crucial presence in the seaside town’s trailblazing creative community ( Barbara Hepworth was an early friend). She was a painter, printmaker, and draftsman who described her practice as a sustained dialogue between inner experience and outer reality. Yet the Tate St Ives exhibition is the first to fully trace the breadth of the Scottish artist’s oeuvre. It features 170 paintings, drawings, and prints that Barns-Graham created over the course of her eight-decade career, alongside rare archival materials. The retrospective spans landscapes, interior paintings, and abstract works, showcasing an artist endlessly attuned to humanity’s profound relationship with the natural world and the boundless possibilities of abstraction evidenced through her insistent probing of line, form, and color. The show brings together rare pieces from private and public collections in order to present the largest survey to date of Barns-Graham’s celebrated “Glacier” series: around 100 paintings the artist began in 1949, following a visit to Switzerland’s Grindelwald Glacier, that experiment with light and geometric forms to convey her encounter with the icy landscape. Amar Kanwar Serpentine Galleries , London Sep. 23, 2026–Jan. 27, 2027 For more than 25 years , Amar Kanwar has pushed the boundaries of documentary filmmaking to meditate on the history, politics, and cultural realities of the Indian subcontinent. He’s earned such recognitions as the MacArthur fellowship (2000) for deeply personal, lyrical films that illuminate contemporary violence, power, and justice. Conceived as a site-specific installation, this major solo exhibition at the Serpentine Galleries brings together three works by the New Delhi–based artist. It includes the feature-length film Such a Morning (2017), in which a renowned mathematician retreats to live in a dark and abandoned train carriage; the multiscreen installation The Peacock’s Graveyard (2023), which blends images and sounds to meditate on the fleeting nature of life; and the debut of a newly commissioned film installation, The Charcoal Man (2026). Three years in the making, it considers how the legacy of the bloody 1947 Partition of India and Pakistan continues to reverberate today. “Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism” Ateneum Art Museum, Helsinki Oct. 23, 2026–Feb. 28, 2027 “Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism” at the Ateneum Art Museum in Helsinki spotlights the work of women artists from Northern Europe, working from the 19th century to today, who were influenced by unorthodox spiritual currents. The role of esotericism on male artists is better known, and the show seeks to expand the public understanding of how these lines of thought shaped their female counterparts. It brings together works by celebrated names such as Hilma af Klint , Ellen Thesleff , and Anna-Eva Bergman alongside lesser-known figures like Ilona Harima, Sonja Ferlov Mancoba , and Maja Fjaestad. Co-curated by Nina Kokkinen, a researcher of art and religion, and Marja Lahelma, chief curator at the Ateneum, the exhibition features artists working across a range of media, including textiles, ceramics, painting, and metal engraving. Highlights include Hilma af Klint’s The Dove No. 1, Series UW, Group 9 (1915), part of the Swedish artist’s widely celebrated project “Paintings for the Temple,” and Oasis (1935) by Danish artist Rita Kernn-Larsen , one of the few renowned female artists to take part in the Surrealist movement during the 1930s. Alvaro Barrington Limbo Museum, Accra Oct. 29, 2026–Feb. 1, 2027 Multidisciplinary artist Alvaro Barrington works with materials like burlap and tarpaulin, which evoke his Caribbean upbringing and the migrant experience. Born in Venezuela and raised between Grenada, Brooklyn, and London, the artist draws on this layered upbringing to create paintings, installations, and embroideries that celebrate community, explore migration and belonging, and defy categorization. Following a residency at Accra’s Limbo Museum, Barrington will present his first solo show on the African continent. The artist has responded to the museum’s raw, permanently incomplete state to realize his institutional commission, which comprises paintings, sculptures, and site-specific installations. He’s developed them with local materials, fabricators, artisans, structures, and modes of production. The exhibition allows the city itself to become an active participant in his process. “Myths and Monsters: the Art of Fantasy in Asia” M + , Hong Kong Oct. 17, 2026–Apr. 4, 2027 “Myths and Monsters: the Art of Fantasy in Asia” reveals how Asian artists have constructed imaginary worlds amid difficult social and political realities. The show unites more than 400 works spanning contemporary art, architecture, fashion, video games, and film; Surrealist dreamscapes, Tibetan Buddhist scrolls, and anime trace the myriad forms fantasy has taken across the region’s visual traditions. Considering the increasingly prominent role of avatars and other digital imagery in Asian daily life, the show also asks why fantasy still matters to how we see the world today. Highlights include Golden Fighter’s Despair (2004), from Cao Fei ’s acclaimed “Cosplayers” series, which explores Chinese youth subcultures cosplaying as anime characters against the backdrop of an increasingly urban and isolating country; Landscape of Self Portrait (1962) by Korean artist Kim Younghwan, a rare exponent of Surrealism who favored dreamlike worlds in defiance of the traditional art trends that prevailed during Korea’s post-liberation era; and Night March of Hundred Monsters (2021–25), a multichannel video and animation installation by Singaporean artist Ho Tzu Nyen that connects Japanese folkloric monsters and the lived horrors of Japanese imperialism in World War II–era Southeast Asia. Giuseppe Penone “The Inner Flow of Life” National Museum of Qatar, Qatar Oct. 26, 2026–Feb. 13, 2027 Giuseppe Penone’ s belief that everything is connected undergirds his multidisciplinary practice. A key exponent of Arte Povera , the radical Italian movement that sought to reconsider the value of humble materials, Penone has worked for more than 50 years. His media have included paper, photography, and performance, with a particular focus on sculpture. Frequent themes include aging, growth, and respiration. “Giuseppe Penone: The Inner Flow of Life” will transform the National Museum of Qatar’s Baraha and Old Palace through a series of pavilions, sculptures, and immersive installations. The artist will install two massive bronze tree sculptures from his “Idee di Pietra (Ideas of Stones)” series at Doha’s Old Port. The exhibition will include work spanning 1969 through today as it highlights Penone’s enduring interest in the synergy between organic and artistic processes. Pieces in wood, iron, water, bronze, clay, and marble will be on view. Correction: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that Giuseppe Penone’s show was co-produced with the Serpentine Galleries in London.

title: Metropolitan Museum of Art cancels its planned John Galliano Costume Institute exhibition.
summary: The Metropolitan Museum of Art will not stage its planned John Galliano retrospective, the museum and the designer announced jointly on Monday, August 31st. “John Galliano: Horizons,” scheduled to open in May 2027 as the Costume Institute’s spring show, has been called off after months of mounting criticism over Galliano’s history of antisemitic and racist remarks. “Following thoughtful discussions with John Galliano, we have together decided not to proceed with the exhibition,” said Max Hollein, the Met’s director and CEO, in a statement. The museum said it will announce a new spring exhibition and details of the 2027 Met Gala at a later date. This year’s show, “Costume Art,” opened in May and runs through January 10, 2027. Galliano said he had made the decision “with great sadness.” “I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it,” he said. “I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture.” The 2027 gala, held as always on the first Monday in May, would have fallen on Yom HaShoah, the Holocaust remembrance day. He added that he did not want the debate around him “to place The Met in a difficult position or to distract from the remarkable work of the Costume Institute,” and that he recognized an exhibition honoring his work “would be painful for some.” Dior dismissed Galliano in 2011 after video surfaced of the designer making antisemitic remarks, including “I love Hitler,” at a Paris café. A French court later convicted him of public insults based on origin, religion, race, or ethnicity. He apologized, entered rehab, and returned as creative director of Maison Margiela from 2014 to 2024. He has spoken publicly about his recovery from alcoholism and addiction. Opposition has built since the museum announced the show in July. The New York Times reported last week that several donors had warned they would pull promised gifts, among them Arne Glimcher, founder of Pace Gallery . In an email to Met curator David Breslin quoted by the Times , Glimcher wrote: “I don’t think you have considered the cost of this action and its reverberations to come.” Critics also included Julie Menin, speaker of New York’s City Council, who called the exhibition “a serious mistake” in a letter to the exhibition’s organizers.

title: MoMA to present major survey of post-colonial African art in 2027.
summary: The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) will present “Freedom and Futures: Emancipatory Art in Africa, 1956–1982,” an exhibition tracing the history of modern art during Africa’s independence era, on view May 2–August 14, 2027. The show brings together roughly 250 objects from collections around the world, including some 40 works from MoMA’s own holdings. The show is organized by curator Ugochukwu-Smooth C. Nzewi with former curatorial associate Erica DiBenedetto. The exhibition proposes “emancipatory art” as a framework for understanding how artists across the continent gave aesthetic form to decolonization. The show describes these works as a form of “emancipatory modernism.” It is organized around two foundational Pan-African gatherings held in Europe— the First Congress of Black Writers and Artists (Paris, 1956) and the Second Congress of Black Writers and Artists (Rome, 1959). These seminal gatherings were followed by five subsequent festivals held in Zimbabwe, Senegal, Algeria, Nigeria, and Botswana between 1962 and 1982. Works from each of these festivals will appear sequentially across six thematic sections spanning painting, sculpture, photography, film, tapestry, and printmaking. Highlights from the show include the Algerian artist Mohammed Khadda ’s Africa Before One (1963), which draws on Tassili cave petroglyphs and Amazigh and Arabic scripts; Nigerian artist Uche Okeke ’s Women Riot (1965), depicting the 1929 women’s tax revolt in eastern Nigeria; Mozambican artist Valente Malangatana ’s surrealist Cry of Freedom (1973), made during the final years of Portuguese colonial rule; and Senegalese artist Iba N'Diaye ’s Juan de Pareja Menaced by Dogs (1982), which reworks a 1650 Diego Velázquez ’ portrait into a statement on neocolonialism. Ahead of the exhibition, MoMA made several significant acquisitions, including works by Khadda, Malangatana, Okeke, Mahjoub Ben Bella , Gavin Jantjes , Gazbia Sirry , and Ibrahim El Salahi . Nzewi sees these acquisitions in the lineage of the museum’s founding director Alfred H. Barr Jr.'s 1960 acquisition of Tanzanian artist Sam Joseph Ntiro's painting Men Taking Banana Beer to Bride by Night (1956) , one of the first acquisitions of a modern work by an African-born artist by a major Western institution, made the same year 17 African nations gained independence. “Freedom and Futures” caps a three-part series on mid-century Africa at MoMA, growing out of the museum’s Contemporary and Modern Art Perspectives (C-MAP) Africa research group, which Nzewi leads. It follows “Ideas of Africa: Portraiture and Political” (on view December 2025–July 2026), which examined Pan-African photographic portraiture drawn largely from collector Jean Pigozzi’s 2019 gift to the museum, and “Architects of Liberation.” Modernism in Western”(on view July 2026–January 2027), which surveyed independence-era architecture across seven West African nations.

title: An Art Lover’s Guide to Seoul
summary: Ask any Seoullite, and they’ll tell you the city is unrecognizable from five years ago. South Korea’s cultural and creative output—music, film, TV, art—has moved from regional strength to global fixture, and Seoul’s art scene has moved with it. The 2022 arrival of Frieze Seoul catalyzed a wave of overseas galleries opening branches in the city, and the influx has drawn foreign collectors deeper into the local scene and toward younger Korean artists working across a widening range of disciplines and media. “For collectors, some of the deepest rewards lie here: not only in recognizing what has already been established, but in encountering a practice before it settles into consensus,” says Hyeyoung Cho, curator of Frieze Seoul’s new Material Practices section. The Dansaekhwa and Mono-ha masters of the 20th century still anchor the historical picture, but for the first time, the story of Korean contemporary art is being written in real time, in Seoul, and for a global audience that’s paying attention. The key neighborhoods for art lovers in Seoul Seoul’s art scene sprawls from Jongno at the historic center, with distinct clusters in Samcheong and Seongbuk to the north, Hannam to the south along the Han River, and pockets pushing outward into Mapo. Samcheong On the right side of Gyeongbokgung—the royal palace of the Joseon Dynasty—Samcheong’s streets are lined with hanok -style walls and kiwa roofs. Fashion designer Jaden Cho, who works in the area, says the walk from Seochon through Gyeongbokgung to Samcheong represents “Seoul’s past and present.” That’s true of its art scene too: Veteran galleries have shaped the Korean canon here since the 1970s and ’80s. Hakgojae , Kukje Gallery , and Gallery Hyundai —the neighborhood’s mainstays—helped make the likes of Lee Jung Seob, Nam June Paik , Lee Ufan , Kim Whanki , and Ha Chong-hyun the modern masters they are today. Other galleries in the area include PKM and Baik Art. WWNN , one of the most talked-about younger galleries, adds vibrancy to the mix. Art Sonje Center focuses on multimedia, performance, and installation work; its collection includes works by Lee Bul , Woo Hannah , and Koo Jeong A . Down toward the Cheonggye stream, Ilmin Museum of Art is led by innovative, interdisciplinary curatorial choices that rarely miss the cultural moment. Seongbuk With Bukhan and Bugak Mountains as its backdrop and several foreign embassies scattered around it, Seongbuk rose in the late 20th century as one of Seoul’s most affluent areas with grand detached houses on winding streets (remember that scene in Parasite ?). Its quiet character and proximity to Daehakro, historically a theater and performance-arts hub, drew artists to live and work there. Wooson Gallery boasts an influential cluster of collectors from Daegu in the country’s southeast; local tastemaker Jason Haam sits nearby. A 10-minute taxi brings you to A-Lounge Contemporary , the Whanki Museum , and Primary Practice on the other side of the mountain. Expect a mix of Korean and international contemporaries in impressive gallery spaces. The hills are steep, so taxis are essential once you’re up there. Hannam If you want off-kilter and sophisticated in one afternoon, Hannam’s the pick. Its international character, enhanced by neighboring Itaewon, where foreigners have lived since the early 20th century, is why many overseas blue-chip galleries have landed here. Begin at Esther Schipper and ThisWeekendRoom , then move down toward Thaddaeus Ropac , Duarte Sequeria , and Foundry . Nearby you’ll also find Lehmann Maupin —among the first overseas arrivals a decade ago—local mainstay Gallery Joeun , Gallery Baton , Pace Gallery , and Gladstone Gallery . The hipster-cool spilling into nearby Yongsan has drawn younger galleries too. Cylinder 2 has been praised for a distinctive style and a wide-ranging collector base (Cylinder 1 sits near Seoul National University). Beyond If you want something rougher around the edges, head to Euljiro , the industrial high street (printing shops, steel merchants) where lower rents have made it a breeding ground for experimental galleries like N/A . West of the city, the Mapo district contains hip pockets such as Mangwon, Sangsu, and Yeonhui. And in Gangnam, the city’s upscale district is home to galleries including White Cube , Perrotin , Opera Gallery , Tang Contemporary Art , Roy Gallery , and G Gallery . The key museums and institutions to know in Seoul Seoul’s institutional depth spans from Joseon-era Korean art to some of the most ambitious contemporary museum programming in East Asia. National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul (MMCA): The city’s flagship contemporary institution is in Samcheong. Its permanent collection features major Korean art from the 1960s to 2010s, while its exhibitions highlight cutting-edge Korean and international contemporary art. Kansong Art Museum: South Korea’s first private museum was founded in Seongbuk in 1938. Kansong Chun Hyung-pil’s collection of Korean cultural heritage remains a rare window into the country's classical art history. Other institutions worth checking out include: Park Seo-Bo Museum: Opening in late August in Yeonhui, this spot is dedicated to one of Korea’s most celebrated modern painters and a key figure of the Dansaekhwa movement. Arumjigi Foundation: The foundation’s Jongno space houses rotating exhibitions on Korea's traditional culture inside a modern building—with a hanok on the rooftop as a surprise. Open to the public for only a couple of months in fall, and per architectural designer Minsung Son, “one of the most magical experiences in Seoul—not to be missed.” National Folk Museum of Korea: On the grounds of Gyeongbokgung in Samcheong, the museum traces Korean folk life, traditional customs, and material culture, a rich counterpoint to the contemporary galleries surrounding it. Free admission. Seoul Museum of Art (SeMA): The city’s flagship public contemporary art museum, near Deoksugung Palace, with rotating exhibitions and a collection focused on Korean and international contemporary work. Amorepacific Museum of Art (APMA): The corporate museum inside David Chipperfield’s Amorepacific headquarters in Yongsan pairs Korean traditional art with contemporary programming, in a building that's a destination in its own right. Frieze House Seoul: The fair’s year-round Seoul outpost programmes exhibitions, talks, and dinners between the annual September edition. A useful drop-in for a read on what Frieze is looking at in Korea now. And an off-the-radar pick: The late painter Kim Tschang-yeul ’s former residence in Seongbuk opened this year as a public space—a rare chance to see where the artist lived and worked. Daeyang Gallery and House , a private gallery and residence designed by Steven Holl and Lee In Ho to look like it’s floating on water, occasionally opens to the public. Where the art world in Seoul eats, drinks, and shops Seoul’s food scene is one of the world’s best. Generations of discerning eaters, high-quality ingredients, and rapid trend cycles converge in the city’s bustling restaurants and cafés. For dinner: For Korean barbecue honed to the finest, Gold Pig Restaurant is Frieze House Seoul director Andy St. Louis’s pick. Reservations are recommended, but walk-ins are not impossible. For Korean contemporary cuisine, MAPS Museum senior curator Seolhui Lee recommends Eatanic Garden , spearheaded by Son Jong-won of Culinary Class Wars fame. If given the chance, try the Pyongyang-style cold noodles. The dish has somehow become the ultimate tastemaker marker among Seoul’s art world. For a vegan-friendly pick, creative producer and filmmaker Eugene Mayu Kim says URT in Hongdae is “always a winner.” For drinks: Bars in Samcheong and Seochon will offer something quieter and more quaint. Gong-Gan , another Lee pick, is a strong cocktail bar for post-opening gatherings. Head south of the river, in Cheongdam district, opposite the Songeun Art and Cultural Foundation, to a refined wine bar, Les Copains , a “haven for discerning oenophiles and post-fair unwinding,” recommended by collector and attorney Jeongho Nam. If you’re open to making the evening a longer one, head to one of the many bars in Haebangchon and continue the night at a club or two in Itaewon. Artist and musician Yubin Choi says of Hertz in Itaewon, “crazy good to see the sunrise.” For coffee: Cafés are their own genre in Seoul. Some attribute the proliferation to the city’s extreme weather. In Euljiro, Choi suggests NETZ kaffeehaus for meetings. MK2 , meanwhile, in Seochon, is loved by nearby architects and design professionals. For browsing: D&DEPARTMENT SEOUL by MMMG offers a snapshot of Korean contemporary craft and design. Minsung Son recommends Oval , “recommended to anyone very particular about their pens, pencils, and paperweights.” For antique furniture, product designer Gyuhan Park points to Dapsimni Antique Market ; for vintage jewelry and watches, Sewoon Square . Haggling is fair game at the traditional markets. Where to stay: Lisa Shin suggests staying at Boan Stay , an accommodation service provided by the art and exhibition space of the same name, with “a beautiful view of the walls and trees of Gyeongbokgung.” Alternatively, consider staying in a hanok -style accommodation, which can be found throughout Jongno, as Wonseok Koh, director of Line Cultural Foundation, recommends. Top tips for art lovers visiting Seoul When to go: Consider early September for Frieze Seoul and Kiaf , the local counterpoint fair. Both draw international curators, artists, and collectors, and together anchor Seoul Art Week, when galleries across the city open new shows. How to navigate: Google Maps is serviceable, but it’s worth downloading Naver Map or Kakao Map instead, recommends Koh. Seoul’s public transit is excellent and often the fastest way to move between clusters, but avoid rush hour where possible. For Seongbuk in particular, taxis are essential given the hills. Plan the day by cluster—Samcheong in the morning, Hannam in the afternoon, for instance—rather than crisscrossing. What locals know: Punctuality is never not fashionable in Korea; always be on time. Openings run late and often spill into dinner and drinks nearby. Seoul is dense despite being smaller than London and New York: Everything takes longer to cross than it looks on the map. Bringing artworks home: Exporting contemporary art from Seoul is straightforward. Most galleries handle international shipping as a matter of course, and Korea’s logistics infrastructure is excellent. English is widely spoken in commercial galleries, especially those with international programs. One thing to verify when buying antique or traditional Korean pieces is whether they are subject to export restrictions, so check the status before buying older work.
